name: doctest
listed_description: Single-header, lightweight, thread-safe C++ unit testing framework with assertions, parameterized tests, reporters and BDD-style tests.
claim_text: Main selling point is that it is the fastest, both at compile time and at runtime, among similarly featured alternatives.
book_benchmark: None. Book states the claim without numbers; the repository README says benchmarks exist.
found_in: book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 10, Runtime testing frameworks, Doctest example

name: [Boost].UT (boost-ext/ut)
listed_description: Single-header or module, macro-free C++20 micro unit testing framework using concepts, source_location and designated initializers.
claim_text: Avoiding a unique type per lambda speeds up compilation by 5x; type-name erasure and memoization also speed up compilation.
book_benchmark: None. Book repeats the design claims without measurements; the repository README links a benchmark against Boost.Test, GoogleTest, Catch and doctest.
found_in: book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 10, Runtime testing frameworks, [Boost].UT example

name: libcds
listed_description: C++ library of concurrent data structures: lock-free queues, stacks, ordered lists, sets and maps, with safe memory reclamation.
found_in: book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 12, Dealing with the drawbacks of concurrency

name: FreeGuard
listed_description: Security-oriented drop-in malloc replacement guarding against heap overflow, use after free and double free; loadable via LD_PRELOAD.
book_benchmark: None. Book cites the project's paper (arXiv 1709.02746, titled as a faster secure heap allocator) but gives no numbers.
guessed_baseline: glibc malloc, DieHarder, other secure allocators
found_in: book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 12, Hardening your code, Security-oriented memory allocator

name: hardened_malloc (GrapheneOS)
listed_description: Actively developed security-focused drop-in malloc for Android Bionic, musl and glibc, based on the OpenBSD malloc design.
found_in: book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 12, Hardening your code, Security-oriented memory allocator

name: Scudo
listed_description: Google user-mode hardened allocator, default in Fuchsia and Android, derived from the LLVM Sanitizers combined allocator, small code and memory footprint.
claim_text: Protects against heap overflow, use after free and double free while maintaining performance; low code and memory footprint.
found_in: book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 12, Hardening your code, Security-oriented memory allocator

name: Binary search (std::lower_bound) versus linear scan (std::find) in a sorted vector, Google Benchmark
listed_description: Book microbenchmark comparing bisection with linear scan over a sorted std::vector of ints at sizes from 1,000 to 10,000,000 and several needle positions.
claim_text: Sample run: binary search 24.2 ns versus linear search 471 ns; with needle at the end of 10M elements, about 24 ns versus 2.8 ms.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark 1.9.4 via Conan, C++20/23, GCC 14+ recommended, DoNotOptimize sink; run on a 20-thread 2022 MHz CPU with 48 KiB L1d and 24 MiB L3; optimization flags not stated. Same benchmark also written with Catch2 and nanobench without printed numbers. Code in Chapter13 of the companion repository.
found_in: book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 13, Measuring performance, Using microbenchmarks

name: C++20 modules replacing header includes for build speed
listed_description: Precompiled binary module interfaces and header units reduce repeated parsing of included headers and speed up C++ builds; book cites an Alibaba Cloud analysis of the gain.
claim_text: Further-reading title: 42% Boost in Compilation Efficiency! A Practical Analysis of C++ Modules (Alibaba Cloud Community blog).
book_benchmark: None in book. Numbers live only in the cited blog post; companion Chapter09 code uses modules without timing.
found_in: book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 9, Introduction to C++ modules; Further reading
